articles.title: I built a background remover that runs 100% in the browser. Here's how I made it 7x faster
articles.description: Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you...
articles.body_html:
Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you to pay for the full-resolution download. I wanted the opposite: the photo never leaves your device, the download is full resolution, and there is no account.

So I built Remove de Fundo, a background remover where the AI model runs entirely in the browser. The first version worked, but on real phones it was slow enough that people left before seeing a result. This post is about what made it slow and what fixed it.

End result on the same laptop and the same photo: 43.8 s → 6.4 s from click to cutout.

The stack

  • Astro for the site (static pages, deployed to Cloudflare Workers)
  • @imgly/background-removal with the IS-Net fp16 model (~88 MB)
  • ONNX Runtime Web, which runs the model with WebGPU on desktop and WebAssembly (CPU) on phones
  • A small post-processing step in canvas to clean up semi-transparent "haze" in the mask

Everything happens client-side. The server only serves static files.

Problem 1: the model came from a CDN that didn't cache

The first visit downloads ~100 MB (model + ONNX runtime). That is unavoidable for an in-browser model, but I noticed something worse: the CDN serving the model sent no Cache-Control header, and the edge marked it cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC. So returning visitors were often downloading the model again, and nothing was cached near the user.

Fix: self-host the model files. A build script downloads the model chunks once and puts them in public/ai/<version>/, and the library is pointed there with publicPath. Since the chunk file names are content hashes, they can be cached forever:

/ai/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Now a returning visitor loads the model from disk cache: zero network.

One gotcha: the chunk files have no extension, and both the dev server and the host treated extensionless paths as pages (404). Saving them as <hash>.bin and rewriting the names in resources.json fixed it.

Problem 2: the CPU path used one core out of eight

Phones always use the WebAssembly path, so CPU speed matters most. ONNX Runtime Web can use multiple threads, but only if the page is cross-origin isolated, because threads need SharedArrayBuffer.

My page wasn't isolated:

crossOriginIsolated // false

Fix: two headers.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless

I used credentialless instead of require-corp so Google Fonts and analytics keep working without CORP headers. Browsers that don't support it simply ignore it, so nothing breaks there.

Result (CPU, model already loaded): 22.7 s → 7.9 s per photo. Almost 3x, from two lines of config.

Problem 3: the bug that made PNG encoding 13x slower

After enabling isolation, inference got much faster but the total barely improved. I logged a timestamp for each stage and found this:

Stage Time
Inference 1.5 s
PNG encode 5.5 s
Edge refinement 4.4 s

Encoding a 1200 × 800 PNG should take a fraction of a second. I measured canvas.convertToBlob() on an idle page:

Page PNG encode
Not isolated 208 ms
Isolated, before loading ONNX 217 ms
Isolated, after running ONNX 2,648 ms

So isolation itself was fine. The problem: the library sets the WASM thread count to navigator.hardwareConcurrency (all cores), and ONNX's worker threads keep spin-waiting after inference. They occupy every core, and the browser's own image-encoding threads starve.

Fix: cap the thread count before the library loads. I used ONNX Runtime's own default (half the cores, at most 4) on CPU, and 1 thread on the GPU path, where the GPU does the work:

function limitOnnxThreads(device: 'gpu' | 'cpu') {
  const cores = navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 4;
  const threads = device === 'gpu' ? 1 : Math.max(1, Math.min(4, Math.ceil(cores / 2)));
  Object.defineProperty(navigator, 'hardwareConcurrency', {
    configurable: true,
    get: () => threads,
  });
}

Post-processing went from ~10 s back to 0.2 s.

Problem 4: the first photo on WebGPU paid for shader compilation

On the WebGPU path, the second photo took 2 s but the first took ~17 s on every page load. The session creation and, mostly, the first inference compile the GPU shaders.

Fix: warm up on intent. When the user hovers the upload area (desktop) or taps it (mobile), I:

  1. Prefetch the model files into the HTTP cache (low priority).
  2. Call the library's preload() with exactly the same config as the real run (the library memoizes the session by JSON.stringify(config)).
  3. On GPU only, run one throwaway inference on a tiny 32×32 image. The model input has a fixed size, so this compiles everything the real photo needs.

While the person is still picking a photo from their gallery, all of that is already happening. I skip the warm inference on CPU: on a phone it would take as long as a real cutout and the user's photo would wait behind it. I also skip prefetching on saveData or 2G connections, and on mobile only a tap on the upload box triggers it, so scrolling past doesn't burn 100 MB of someone's data.

Things I tried that didn't work

  • The smaller quantized model (isnet_quint8, 44 MB). Half the download, but it left patches of background all over a portrait. Not worth it.
  • Relying on HTTP heuristic caching for a third-party CDN. In practice, returning visitors still re-downloaded.

UX fixes that mattered as much as speed

  • The upload box was below the fold on a 730 px laptop screen. People saw a headline and left. Tightening the hero put the button in the first screen on laptops and phones.
  • Show the user's own photo with a scanning line while processing, instead of a generic spinner. It makes the wait feel much shorter.
  • On mobile, the label "Drag your photo here" makes no sense. It now says "Choose a photo".

Results

Before After
Click → result (laptop, first run) 43.8 s 6.4 s
CPU inference per photo 22.7 s 7.9 s
PNG encode + edge cleanup ~10 s (isolated, before fix) 0.2 s
Returning visitor model download often ~100 MB 0 (disk cache)

Since adding analytics, about 98% of removals succeed and more than half of the people who upload a photo download the result.

Credits

The heavy lifting is done by IMG.LY's background-removal-js (AGPL-3.0) and ONNX Runtime Web. If you build something similar, check their licenses.

You can try it here: removedefundo.com/en. It's free, with no sign-up, and works in English, Spanish and Portuguese. I'd love feedback, especially from people on older phones.

This post was written with AI assistance. The numbers come from real measurements on the live site.

articles.title: A VS Code extension to turn ANY free chatbot website into an AI agent (kind of)
articles.description: If you've ever pasted ten files into ChatGPT, asked for a fix, then manually copied the result back...
articles.body_html:
If you've ever pasted ten files into ChatGPT, asked for a fix, then manually copied the result back into ten different files by hand, this post is for you!

Already using ReptClip? Skip the intro and jump straight to what's new in v2.0

The problem

Coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor are great, but they cost money, and not everyone wants (or can afford) a subscription. Meanwhile, free chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude.ai are sitting right there, perfectly capable of writing good code, as long as you can get your project's context in front of them and get the resulting changes back into your files without losing your mind 🤔

That gap, pasting context in and applying diffs back out, is tedious enough that most people just don't bother. They either pay for an agent or they give up and do it manually, file by file.

Enter ReptClip

ReptClip is a free, open source VS Code extension that closes that gap 🙂 It lives right in VS Code's bottom panel, as its own tab next to your terminal, so there's no separate window or webpage to juggle. No API key, no subscription, no vendor lock-in. It works with literally any free chatbot you could find online.

Here's what the whole loop looks like in practice:

Here is the explanation. It's a 3-step process:

  1. Copy context to clipboard. Pick the files you care about (by path or glob pattern), hit the "Context" button, and ReptClip copies your project structure, AI instructions, and the file contents as clean Markdown straight to your clipboard (each section can be easily toggled on/off).
  2. Paste into your chatbot. Drop it into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, whatever you're using, along with your prompt.
  3. Apply the diffs. The chatbot replies with its normal explanation, along with a single code block containing Search/Replace diffs. Copy that block, click "Apply Diffs" in the ReptClip panel, and your files are updated!!! 😎

If the chatbot needs to see more of your project mid-conversation, it can ask for it, and you feed that back in with one more click.

Some things that make it safe to actually trust with your codebase:

  • ReptClip only touches files that are tracked by git. Anything your .gitignore files (at any depth) exclude is completely off-limits, for reading, searching, writing, creating, or deleting. .git folders are always off-limits too. Changing a .gitignore file always asks for confirmation first, since that can un-ignore something that was previously protected. If something ever goes wrong anyway, you can simply discard the changes with git.
  • Applying a diff is all or nothing. If one block fails to match, nothing gets written. Fuzzy matching handles whitespace and line-ending differences, but still requires a unique match.
  • You get 10 levels of Undo/Redo specifically for applied diffs, separate from your normal editor undo.
  • And MUCH more! 🙂 README

The UI state is saved per project automatically, so you don't have to re-enter when you come back or be mixed up with other projects.

How to install

It's available in both VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX. So no problem if you're on a VS Code alternative like Cursor or Windsurf. Simply search "ReptClip" and install.

What's new in v2.0

This is a major version bump. The headline feature is a complete rework of how ReptClip feeds extra context to your chatbot mid-conversation, and it also brings several useful new features for applying diffs 🎉

"More Files" is gone. Say hello to "More Context."

In v1, if the chatbot wanted more files, it would ask for a list of files. That's it. That's all it could ask for.

In v2.0, the chatbot can generate a small command block containing three types of commands, and ReptClip generates the output (no subprocess) and copies it to your clipboard!

  • cat <path> reads a full file.
  • grep <flags> <pattern> [paths...] searches your project's contents, ripgrep-style, running in-process (no subprocess spawned).
  • read-lines <path> <start> [end] pulls a specific, 1-indexed line range out of a file, handy for huge files where you only need a slice.

So instead of the chatbot blindly asking for whole files it might not even need, it can now search your codebase for the right TODO, grep for every usage of a function, or read just the relevant 20 lines of a 2,000-line file. It supports the flags -i, -w, -F, -g, -m, -v, and more. Everything still respects your .gitignore the same way the "Context" button does.

Click "More Context," and it works exactly the way "More Files" used to: read the clipboard, validate everything up front (so a bad path or invalid pattern fails the whole batch with a clear error instead of a half-built result), then build the output and send it back to your clipboard or output file.

Line counts in the project structure

The "Project structure" section now lists each file with its raw line count next to it, like src/main.py (387). This gives the chatbot a much better sense of file size before it decides whether to cat the whole thing or just read-lines a chunk of it. You can turn this off with the new reptclip.showLineCounts setting if you'd rather keep the structure listing minimal.

Move, rename, and explicit delete in diffs

The diff format your chatbot generates picked up two new one-line operations:

  • old/path.txt -> new/path.txt moves or renames a file without touching its contents.
  • old/path.txt delete removes a file outright.

That last one matters because the old behavior changed slightly: an empty REPLACE block used to mean "delete this file," but only if the SEARCH block matched the file's entire current contents. That meant deleting a file required the chatbot to regenerate the whole thing, verbatim, inside the SEARCH block, just to throw it away.

That's wasted tokens at best, and at worst a single mismatched character in a large file would make the whole delete fail to apply. Now the chatbot just writes old/path.txt delete and moves on, no regeneration needed! An empty REPLACE block on its own now just clears the matched text and keeps the file (even if that leaves it empty).

Undo now warns you before it steps on changes

If you hit Undo on an applied diff and the file in question has since been modified, either on disk or with unsaved changes in the editor, ReptClip now shows a warning first instead of silently reverting over your work.

And... I received my first external PR! 🥳

A huge part of making v2.0 safe to ship came from @mansio, who contributed two PRs to effessdev/reptclip, totalling roughly 1,500 lines of code!!! 🤯

The first PR focused on security in the diff-applying process. It uncovered several issues, including symlinks allowing writes outside the workspace, the ability to overwrite .git files, and Undo/Redo overwriting unsaved editor changes. It also fixed a .gitignore parsing bug.

The second PR caught even more edge cases, like missed editor changes on case-insensitive filesystems, race conditions during file updates, and incomplete symlink protection that could expose .git or .env contents to the chatbot. These are now fixed, huge thanks to @mansio! 🎉

A little help goes a long way 🥲

ReptClip wouldn't be quite what it is today without a few people who took the time to share their thoughts and suggestions.

A big shout-out to @unitbuilds for letting me know about the limited-time Qoder promotion. That tip made a huge difference and helped make ReptClip possible! The promotion may be over, but I now have something even better: ReptClip! 😁 In fact, I used ReptClip itself to build ReptClip v2. And I mean heavily! 🤯

Thanks to @piekwerk for actually giving ReptClip a try and suggesting that reverting changes should check for dirty editor tabs. I initially overlooked this, but now I get how important that was. In v2.0, both Undo and Redo now check for changes on disk and unsaved editor changes, warning you before proceeding.

And thanks to both @piekwerk and @mansio for pointing out something I hadn't considered: the order in which files are included in a prompt matters! Long prompts can lose effectiveness when important context gets buried in the middle. That feedback led me to make file patterns respect their written order, so you can push the most important files closer to the end of the context (right before your prompt).

For example:

  • **/*.py main.py: Includes all Python files, but puts main.py last.
  • **/*.py src/**/*.py main.py: Includes all Python files, puts files under src/ after the other Python files, and puts main.py last.

These might seem like small details, but they're exactly the kind of feedback that makes a project better. Thank you all for taking the time to help!

Try it out

Watch how beautifully ReptClip applies a large project reorganization:

Want to try it yourself? Head over to VS Code (or your favourite VS Code alternative), search for "ReptClip", and hit Install! It's that simple 😎

You can also find it on the official pages 🔥:

  • VS Code Marketplace
  • Open VSX Registry
  • GitHub repository

It's free, open source, and works with whatever chatbot you already have open in another tab. If you run into something weird while using it, please open an issue so I can fix it, or create a pull request if you want to fix it yourself 🙂 Reviews are fast right now! ⚡

If ReptClip saves you even one round of manual copy-pasting, or you think it'd be useful for others, the single most useful thing you can do for the project right now is head over to github.com/effessdev/reptclip and hit that ⭐ button! It's free, it takes two seconds, and it's the main way other people stumbling onto this post will know the project is worth a look!

articles.title: I Haven't Written a Line of Code in Months. And I Don't Know How to Feel About It.
articles.description: Introduction   It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a lifetime ago. Our world, and especially our programming world, moves so fast that I can't recognize the way it was 6 years ago, 2 years ago, or even at the beginning of this year. So, I wanted to write down some thoughts and see where they take me.

Dealing with changes

In our line of work, we're used to changes right? New languages, new technologies, new frameworks... we've always had new things to look forward to, or being scared of, learn, hate... But this AI stuff... Damn, it's not just something new, it's the first time I've actually felt threatened, in danger, overwhelmed.

It's a very strange feeling because I have the feeling like we are at the edge of a new world, full of possibilities, adventures, discoveries. Things that we thought would take us weeks, months, or years to do or solve become doable so much faster. In the field of science, we see cool stuff happening. And even if I don't understand anything about it, it looks cool to discover new proofs and solutions, even if it's AI assisted. But...

What about me?

I'm a good developer ok? I'm not a rockstar, but I've some strenghts. I've always enjoyed learning new stuff about design patterns, how to write good code. Less than a year ago, I was still learning new things, trying to write more elegant code. I was happy when I found a beautiful solution to a problem.

Around March this year, our team decided it was time to equip everyone with Claude. I don't think I've written a line of code since then. How insane is that? Most of my time was spent in writing code, and now, it has completely disappeared from my tasks. So now, I'm mostly managing agents and doing all the conception and planning. That's where my "expertise" comes in. Because this stuff writes much better code than me anyway.

I feel... dizzy.

What about my (our) future?

The one thing that is scary is not knowing to me. I don't know what our jobs will look like next year, in 2 years, in 10 years. Will we still have a job? How will it look? I'm not much into the doom prediction like "Developers will be gone in 6 months". But something is gonna change drastically right? What about the juniors, the people entering the job market today?

It's not all bad of course. It's not. It's the uncertainty that's difficult for me.

I'm building a very cool project with a few colleagues and AI allowed us to move a lot faster than we would have on our own. That's really exciting. Being able to deliver features a lot faster to users is always a nice feeling. That's one of the main reasons I started doing this anyway, help people.

Loss of craftsmanship

When I wrote the code, with my slow hands, I felt like a craftsman. I was building something. The code was mine. Now, it's not. It's industrialized. A machine makes it. Like countless other craftsmen in the history of our species, what I used to do with my hands in hours or days is done by a machine in minutes.

It's a strange feeling. Of course, I try to comfort myself. I still need to pilot this thing. It doesn't have my humanity, it doesn't know my users like I know them. I have better business knowledge than this machine. And in the end, it's always me that makes the final decision. For how long? And how much value does it have?

This is also why I write this. Because I can still sit in front of my computer and pour out the words. My words. From my brain and my heart. It feels good to create something all by yourself. And I still have the hope that whatever the future holds for us, we will build cool stuff to help people. I hope that the AI era that we're entering will be a net positive for humanity.

Conclusion

That's it, that was my little rant. I'll keep building things that I believe will help people to better their lives and jobs. We will see, together, where this new world takes us.

Have fun <3

articles.title: The Best Cyberdeck Is Not the Most Powerful One. It Is the One You Actually Carry
articles.description: Power looks great on a spec sheet. It looks terrible at the bottom of a drawer.     Everyone has seen...
articles.body_html:
Power looks great on a spec sheet. It looks terrible at the bottom of a drawer.

Everyone has seen that cyberdeck.

It is beautiful. It is huge. It has a mechanical keyboard that sounds like a thunderstorm, a 10 inch screen, three antennas, a battery pack the size of a brick, and enough RGB to be visible from low orbit. The build log took four months. The photos got 40,000 likes. The comments are all fire emojis and "this is the dream build."

And then it lives in a closet.

Not because it is bad. Because it is uncarryable. It is too heavy for a coffee shop. Too fragile for a backpack. Too conspicuous for a library. Too power hungry to survive a real afternoon away from an outlet. It was built to impress the internet, not to survive Tuesday.

Here is the uncomfortable truth the cyberdeck community does not like to admit: most cyberdecks fail the same way most gym memberships fail. Not from lack of ambition. From lack of friction math.

A cyberdeck is not a desktop. A cyberdeck is a companion. If you do not carry it, it does not exist.

The spec sheet trap

Spec sheets lie by telling the truth.

Yes, that Raspberry Pi 5 with NVMe is faster. Yes, that 16GB of RAM will crush a Pi Zero. Yes, that big display is easier to read. All true. All irrelevant if the thing never leaves your desk.

We have been trained by tech culture to worship maximums. Maximum cores. Maximum storage. Maximum screen. Maximum battery, in theory. But a portable device is not judged by its maximum. It is judged by its minimum viable hassle.

Ask a different set of questions:

How long does it take to go from "I have an idea" to "I am typing"?
How many cables, dongles, and adapters does it need?
Can you use it standing up?
Can you use it with one hand while holding coffee in the other?
Will you feel weird pulling it out in public?
Will it still be alive in three hours without hunting for a plug?

If the answer to any of those is no, you did not build a cyberdeck. You built a luggable desktop with extra steps.

The best deck is not the one that wins a benchmark. It is the one that wins the moment you decide to bring it.

Carryability is a feature, not a compromise

We treat small, light, and simple like apologies. Like we settled. Like we could not afford the real build.

Flip that.

Carryability is engineering. It is the hardest engineering in the whole project, because it forces you to make choices. A big deck lets you avoid choices. You just add more. More battery, more screen, more ports, more weight. A small deck forces you to decide what actually matters.

What do you actually do on a cyberdeck?

Be honest. Not the fantasy version where you are wardriving across the city while cracking Wi-Fi and live-streaming from a rooftop. The real version.

You take notes. You check a sensor. You SSH into something. You run a quick scan. You write a little code. You read documentation offline. You test a gadget. You journal. You mess around. You learn.

Almost none of that needs a flagship processor. Almost all of it needs instant on, good battery, a keyboard you can actually type on, and a screen you can read in sunlight or in a dim cafe.

The deck that does those five things every single day will teach you more, help you build more, and make you a better hacker than the monster deck that does everything in theory and nothing in practice.

Power is a party trick. Portability is a habit.

The three laws of a deck you will carry

After building, breaking, rebuilding, and abandoning more decks than I want to admit, I landed on three rules. They are not sexy. They work.

1. If it needs a bag, it is already losing.

The best cyberdeck fits in a jacket pocket, a small sling, or the side pocket you already use. Not a dedicated Pelican case. Not a backpack with a custom foam insert. Not a tote bag you have to remember.

The moment a device requires its own logistics, your brain starts negotiating. "Do I really need it today?" "It is kind of heavy." "I will just use my phone." And you lose. Every time.

A pocketable deck changes your relationship to it. You bring it because it is already there. You use it because the friction is zero. You find uses for it you never planned for, because it is present when life happens.

That is why the ESP32 handhelds and the Cardputer style builds punch so far above their weight. They are not trying to replace your laptop. They are trying to be there when your laptop is not.

2. Battery life beats processing power, every time.

A dead supercomputer is a paperweight. A live microcontroller is a tool.

People obsess over CPU and ignore the only spec that determines whether you get to use the thing: how long it runs, and how fast it charges.

A good carry deck should survive a full day of light use. Not "a full day if you turn the brightness down and do nothing." A real day. Notes, scans, terminal sessions, a little Wi-Fi tinkering, some idle time while you think.

That usually means you need to be ruthless about the screen, the radio, and the software. A smaller screen sips power. An e-ink or low-power LCD sips even less. Turning off Wi-Fi when you are not using it is not a compromise, it is a superpower. Running lean software instead of a full desktop environment is not primitive, it is smart.

The irony is that the "less powerful" deck often feels faster in the field, because it is awake, responsive, and ready. The powerful deck is still booting, still updating, still asking for a password, still dying at 34 percent.

3. It has to survive being used, not just being photographed.

Build photos are taken on clean desks. Real life is not a clean desk.

Real life is rain. Real life is a backpack full of cables that will scratch anything. Real life is dropping it on concrete. Real life is crumbs. Real life is a coffee spill. Real life is a friend picking it up and immediately pressing every button.

If your deck cannot survive that, it is a museum piece.

This is where the maker aesthetic actually matters. A 3D printed case with a little flex is better than a perfect CNC shell you are afraid to scratch. A screen protector you do not care about is better than a gorgeous bare screen you baby. A keyboard you can replace for 12 dollars is better than a custom keyboard you will cry over.

Build it to be scuffed. Build it to be repaired. Build it to be boring enough that you are not scared to use it.

The decks that last are not the prettiest ones. They are the ones with duct tape, a replaced screw, a slightly melted corner, and a story.

The fantasy build vs. the field build

Let us compare two imaginary builders. We all know both of them. We have been both of them.

Fantasy Builder starts with a parts list from a viral video. Pi 5, NVMe hat, 7 inch touchscreen, full size mechanical keyboard, RTL-SDR, big battery, 3D printed cyberpunk case with six antennas. Cost: 450 dollars. Build time: three weekends. Weight: almost 4 pounds.

He finishes it. He posts it. It blows up. He uses it twice at his desk to show friends. Then it goes on a shelf, because taking it anywhere feels like moving house.

Field Builder starts with a question: what do I want to do when I am away from my desk? Her answer is simple: take notes, run terminal stuff, test ESP32 sensors, and have something offline to tinker with.

She builds small. ESP32-S3 or a Pi Zero class board, a tiny keyboard, a small display, a 3D printed case that fits in her jacket. Cost: under 120 dollars. Build time: one afternoon. Weight: less than a paperback.

She carries it everywhere. To the park. To the bus stop. To work. She uses it to log sensor data on a walk. She uses it to sketch out a project while waiting for coffee. She breaks it, fixes it, upgrades one part at a time.

Six months later, who is the better hacker? Who has built more? Who actually understands their hardware?

It is not close. Field Builder wins, because she has six months of reps and Fantasy Builder has six months of dust.

Reps beat specs. Always.

What to actually prioritize

If you are building your first deck, or rebuilding the one that lives in your closet, here is the priority order that actually matters in the field. In order.

1. Keyboard and input.
If typing sucks, you will not write. If you will not write, you will not use it. A small but tactile keyboard beats a big mushy touchscreen every time. Test it. Type a paragraph. Type code. If your thumbs cramp in two minutes, it is the wrong keyboard.

2. Screen readability.
Not size. Readability. Can you read it outdoors? Can you read it at low brightness to save battery? Is the text sharp enough that you do not get a headache? A tiny sharp screen you can read beats a big washed out screen you squint at.

3. Battery and charging.
USB-C. Common cells. Easy to swap or top up from a power bank you already own. If it needs a weird charger, you will forget that charger. If it needs a weird battery, you will stop replacing it.

4. Durability and repairability.
Screws, not glue. A case you can reprint. Parts you can buy again. A design you can open without breaking. Your future self will thank you when something inevitably snaps.

5. Software simplicity.
One home screen. A few tools you actually use. Offline first. No 20 minute boot ritual. No dependency hell every time you turn it on. The best field software is boring, stable, and fast.

Notice what is not on that list: raw CPU power, RAM, storage size, number of ports, RGB, or antenna count. Those are nice. They are not the foundation. Build the foundation first, then add flair if you still want it and it does not break the first five.

The case for the "dumb" deck

There is a growing movement toward dumber, smaller, more focused devices, and it is not nostalgia. It is a reaction to bloat.

Your phone already does everything. It is a supercomputer with a great camera and infinite distractions. Your laptop already does everything else. What is missing is not another everything device. What is missing is a something device.

A deck that does one or two things really well, offline, without notifications, without an app store begging for attention.

An ESP32 anti-phone style handheld that is just for notes, terminal, and sensor tinkering. A BRUCE style tool that is just for wireless research. A biosphere deck that is just for watching a plant and learning about telemetry. These sound limited on paper. In practice, limitation is focus. Focus is what makes you actually finish a project instead of doomscrolling on a bigger screen.

The dumb deck respects your attention. It does not try to be your whole digital life. It tries to be a good tool for a specific kind of curiosity.

That is why so many of us end up loving the small builds. They do not compete with our phones. They complement them. They give us a place to think without being pulled into the feed.

How to rescue the deck you already built

If you already have a big deck gathering dust, do not scrap it. Shrink its job.

Take it apart, mentally. What is the one thing on it you actually loved? The keyboard? The screen? The radio? The battery setup?

Build a tiny version around just that one thing. Use the big deck as your home base station. Let it be the thing that flashes firmware, stores files, and does heavy work at your desk. Let the small deck be the thing that goes out into the world.

Most makers do not need one perfect deck. They need a system: a small carry deck, and a bigger home deck. The small one collects ideas and data. The big one processes them.

That is a much healthier way to think about it. You are not downsizing. You are specializing.

And if you are starting from scratch, start small on purpose. Start with the smallest deck that can do the thing you care about most. Use it for a month. Write down every moment you wished it did something else. Those notes are your real spec sheet. Not a YouTube video. Not a Reddit thread. Your actual life.

Build version two from those notes. Not from FOMO.

The real flex

The real flex in the cyberdeck world is not the most expensive build. It is the most used build.

It is the deck with the worn keys. The deck with the scratched case. The deck with the weird sticker and the replaced battery and the custom script that only makes sense to you. The deck that has been to the park and the bus and the basement and the cafe. The deck that has actually lived.

Anyone can buy parts and assemble a showpiece. It takes discipline to build something small enough, simple enough, and tough enough that you will actually carry it every day.

So ask yourself the honest question before your next build: am I building this to post, or am I building this to carry?

If it is to post, go big. Go wild. Have fun. No judgment. We all love a beautiful build log.

But if it is to carry, go small. Go simple. Go durable. Go boring in the best way. Build the deck that disappears into your pocket and reappears exactly when you need it.

Because the best cyberdeck is not the one with the best specs.

It is the one that is with you when the idea hits.

Keep building.

If this hit you in the chest a little, it is probably because you have a deck in a drawer right now. Go get it. Shrink it, fix it, or rebuild it smaller. Then actually take it outside.

For deeper build guides, field manuals, and hands-on projects, check the guides on Gumroad:

Relevant guides from numbpilled.gumroad.com:

articles.description: All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself....
articles.body_html:
All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself.

georgekobaidze / dotnet11-playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

.NET 11 & C# 15 Playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

Use it to explore language changes, try out APIs, and validate ideas in isolation without production constraints. Each feature lives in its own small project, often with a "before" and "after" version so you can see what the new feature actually changes.

What's inside

Project Feature Description
Unions Union types A small console login flow that compares the classic class-hierarchy approach with C# 15 unions and compiler-checked exhaustive matching.

More examples will be added as new features are explored.

Getting started

You'll need the .NET 11 SDK. Then clone the repo and run any example:

dotnet run --project src/Unions

Disclaimer

.NET 11 and C# 15 features may still change. The code here is for learning and experimentation, not production use.


View on GitHub


Follow me on GitHub for more updates!

Table of Contents

  • Unions Aren't Magic
  • What You'll Need
  • Opening the DLL
    • Decompiling with ILSpy
    • The First Surprise
  • Breaking Down the Struct
    • [Union]: A Label for the Compiler
    • struct: A Value Type
    • IUnion and Value: One Slot for Every Case
    • One Constructor per Case
  • Where the Conversions Happen
  • What a Switch on a Union Becomes
  • Wrapping Up

Unions Aren't Magic

Unions are great. You declare a type in one line and the compiler checks every switch expression for you, and the "impossible" branch finally stays impossible. Joy of joys!

But unions aren't magic. There's no new runtime type, no special instruction in the CLR, and no hidden framework doing the work at runtime. Everything happens at compile time. The compiler takes your one-line union declaration and turns it into ordinary C# that .NET has understood for years.

So what does that ordinary code look like?

In the previous article of this series, we looked at what unions are, how to use them, and whether we actually need them. This time, we're going to pop the hood. We'll take the project from the previous article, open its compiled DLL, and look at what the compiler really generates when you write union.

Major spoiler alert: it's a struct.

What You'll Need

You don't need much to follow along:

  • .NET 11 SDK. Run dotnet --list-sdks and check that you see 11.0.x.
  • VS Code with the C# Dev Kit extension, or any other .NET IDE.
  • A way to see IL. In VS Code, install the ILSpy .NET Decompiler extension (icsharpcode.ilspy-vscode). ILSpy also runs as a standalone app.

If you use JetBrains Rider, you don't need anything extra: it has a built-in IL Viewer that shows the IL for the code under your cursor, and it can also decompile assemblies.

  • The project from the previous article. Clone the repository and build it in Release mode: 
git clone https://github.com/georgekobaidze/dotnet11-playground.git
cd dotnet11-playground
dotnet build -c Release

Why Release? Debug builds add extra instructions and variables to make debugging easier. Release shows you what actually ships.

After the build, the compiled DLL is at src/Unions/bin/Release/net11.0/Unions.dll. That's the file we're going to open.

Opening the DLL

Let's start with the union from the previous article. Here's its source code, from src/Unions/LoginService/LoginAfter.cs:

public record LoggedIn(string UserName);
public record InvalidCredentials(int AttemptsLeft);
public record AccountLocked(DateTimeOffset Until);
public record TwoFactorRequired(string Method);

public union LoginResult(LoggedIn, InvalidCredentials, AccountLocked, TwoFactorRequired);

Four records and one line that groups them. Now let's see what that line turned into.

Decompiling with ILSpy

  1. Open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) and type ILSpy.
  2. Choose the command that opens an assembly, and pick src/Unions/bin/Release/net11.0/Unions.dll.
  3. A new ILSpy: Assemblies view appears in the Explorer. Expand Unions, then the Unions.After namespace, and find LoginResult.
  4. Click it. ILSpy decompiles it and shows the result in an editor tab.

By default, ILSpy shows decompiled C#. To see the raw IL, click the Output: C# … item in VS Code's status bar (bottom right) and pick IL. We'll use both: C# to understand the shape of the type, and IL to see exactly what the compiler emitted.

The First Surprise

The project has two types called LoginResult, one from each version of the login code:

  • Unions.Before.LoginResult is the abstract record we used before C# 15.
  • Unions.After.LoginResult is the union.

First let's look at the decompiled C# code of the old LoginResult:

It's an abstract record, just like in the source code.

Now let's look at the new LoginResult.

As you can see here, it's a struct behind the mask. Unions, you've been exposed.

That's the main idea of this article: there's no "union" in the compiled code. The runtime has never heard of unions. There's only an ordinary struct that the compiler wrote for you.

And now let's look at the IL code.

A quick warning about the IL view: don't try to read it line by line. IL is a low-level, stack-based instruction set written for the runtime, not for humans. Skim it for the parts we care about (the type declaration, its attributes, and the method signatures) and leave the rest to the JIT compiler.

Now let's break this struct down piece by piece and see what each part does.

Breaking Down the Struct

Let's go through the generated LoginResult from top to bottom.

[Union]: A Label for the Compiler 

[Union]
public struct LoginResult : IUnion

The first thing on the type is the [Union] attribute. It comes from System.Runtime.CompilerServices, which is why ILSpy added that using at the top of the file.

The attribute doesn't do anything at runtime. It's a label for the compiler. When another project references Unions.dll and uses LoginResult, the compiler reads this attribute and knows to treat the struct as a union: it allows the implicit conversions and checks your switch expressions for exhaustiveness.

It also means the union keyword isn't the only way to get a union. Any struct or class with the [Union] attribute and the right shape (single-parameter constructors and a Value property) gets the same treatment. Union libraries can use this to plug into the compiler's checks without users switching to the new syntax.

struct: A Value Type

The compiler chose a struct, not a class. That means a LoginResult variable holds the union directly, not a reference to it, and creating one doesn't allocate a separate wrapper object on the heap. The wrapper is just one field, as we'll see in a moment.

IUnion and Value: One Slot for Every Case 

public object? Value { get; }

This is the heart of the union. There's one property, and it holds whichever case is current. Look at the assembly tree: there's only one field, <Value>k__BackingField, the compiler-generated storage behind this auto-property. That's why a union can never hold two cases at once: there's simply nowhere to put the second one.

Notice the type: object?. At runtime, the struct doesn't know or care that Value can only be a LoggedIn, InvalidCredentials, AccountLocked or TwoFactorRequired. That rule exists only at compile time. The compiler enforces it, and the generated code just stores an object.

The property is also get-only, so a union can't change after it's created. The IL backs this up: the backing field is marked initonly (IL's version of readonly), and the getter carries an IsReadOnly attribute. When you assign a new case to a variable, you replace the whole struct.

The IUnion interface is the contract behind this property. Any union, whether declared with union or hand-written with [Union], exposes its current case through Value.

One Constructor per Case 

[CompilerGenerated]
public LoginResult(LoggedIn value)
{
    Value = value;
}

The compiler generated one constructor for each case type: LoggedIn, InvalidCredentials, AccountLocked, and TwoFactorRequired. Each one does exactly one thing: it stores the value in Value. The [CompilerGenerated] attribute marks them as code you didn't write yourself.

These constructors are where the implicit conversions come from. We'll see them in action in a moment.

It also explains why only the listed types are accepted. There's no LoginResult(string) constructor, so there's no conversion from string.

Where the Conversions Happen

Remember this line from AuthService.Login?

return new InvalidCredentials(MaxAttempts - failed);

The method returns a LoginResult, but we return an InvalidCredentials. Open Unions.After → AuthService → Login(string, string) in ILSpy to see how that works:

There's no magic conversion. The compiler simply wrapped the record in one of the constructors we saw earlier, the one that takes an InvalidCredentials. That's why we didn't have to change a single line of AuthService in the previous article. (And if you're wondering where MaxAttempts went: it's a const, so the compiler replaced it with its value, 3.) In the IL view, you'll see it as a newobj instruction calling LoginResult::.ctor.

What a Switch on a Union Becomes

Now for the part that makes unions worth using: the exhaustive switch. Our top-level code in Program.cs compiles into a hidden Program class with a <Main>$ method. You'll find it under the empty namespace node ({ }) in the assembly tree.

The compiler copies loginResult.Value into a local variable, and the switch expression becomes a series of type checks on Value: is it a LoggedIn? An InvalidCredentials? An AccountLocked? A TwoFactorRequired?

Look closely: our exhaustive switch expression turned into a chain of nested if/else checks. That's the exact form that doesn't get exhaustiveness checking when you write it yourself. The safety comes from what you write, not from what runs.

So where's the exhaustiveness? It's not in the output. It was checked at compile time and then thrown away. The runtime never sees it, which is why the compiler still adds one last branch: if none of the type checks match, it calls a compiler-generated helper that throws a SwitchExpressionException. That branch runs only in one situation: an empty, default union whose Value is null.

The compiler checks your work. The runtime just runs plain type checks.

Wrapping Up

We popped the hood, and here's what we found: unions aren't magic. They're a compiler feature, not a runtime feature.

When you write one line:

public union LoginResult(LoggedIn, InvalidCredentials, AccountLocked, TwoFactorRequired);

the compiler turns it into an ordinary struct:

  • a [Union] attribute and the IUnion interface, so the compiler recognizes it as a union,
  • a single object? Value property that holds the current case,
  • and one constructor per case type, which is where the implicit conversions come from.

Your switch expressions become plain type checks on Value. The exhaustiveness check, the feature that makes unions worth using, happens entirely at compile time. By the time your code runs, it's gone.

Knowing this explains a few things that might otherwise feel strange:

  • Why default is empty. It's a struct, and every struct has a default value.
  • Why value-type cases get boxed. Everything is stored in an object?.
  • Why switch expressions matter. The compiler can only check what it sees at compile time. Write the same logic as an if/else chain or a classic switch statement, and that check is gone.

None of this makes unions less useful. It makes them predictable. You now know exactly what you're shipping.

I have to admit: in the AI era, there's something incredibly satisfying about digging through low-level IL code yourself.

If you haven't read it yet, start with the first article to see unions in action. All the code from both articles is in the GitHub repository. Clone it, open Unions.dll in ILSpy or Rider, and pop the hood yourself.

What surprised you most about what the compiler generates? Let me know in the comments.

articles.title: Riemann Hypothesis Lean proof: what the checkers actually check
articles.description: A 17.4M-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis compiles. What Lean, nanoda, con-leche and lake comparator check, and what is still open.
articles.body_html:
The Riemann Hypothesis Lean proof that Levent Alpöge posted on November 20, 2026 is 17.4 million lines of code in 175,187 files, and it compiles. Strangers have built it, several independently written checkers accept the exported proof, and one check was still running when I last looked on Saturday afternoon (GMT+7). This post explains what each of those checks covers, what it leaves open, and what a developer can reuse from the way people are checking AI-written proofs.

Everything below is a claim under review, and no part of it is an accepted result yet. I use "claims", "compiles" and "accepts" on purpose.

TL;DR

  • Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note saying he believes he has, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization, and released only Lean code (note).
  • Andrew Sutherland of MIT reports that all 175,187 modules compile with zero errors, and that the five headline theorems use only the three standard axioms (MIT verification page).
  • Kernels written by other people accept the 61.6 GB export: nanoda in 27 minutes 42 seconds and con-leche in 3 minutes 15 seconds.
  • As of Saturday November 21, 17:05 GMT+7, the official lake comparator run on the full proof and the Lean kernel replays were still running. Its statement comparison and axiom check had passed in one run, and con-leche's compare mode accepted all five theorems.
  • Nobody has digested the argument yet. Terence Tao wrote that this will take some time.

What the Riemann Hypothesis Lean proof actually contains

Alpöge's note says Claude "flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line", and that a prose version he generated hit more than 250,000 pages, which he called slop. He posted none of it. What exists is a Lean archive split into 14 parts, about 239 MB compressed, 17,374,215 lines in 175,187 files according to the import analysis people posted on the Lean Zulip thread.

Lean is a proof assistant. You write a statement and a proof, and a small program called the kernel checks every step against a short list of rules. If the kernel accepts, the statement follows from the axioms you allowed. The Riemann Hypothesis here is Mathlib's own definition, which in Lean reads that every nontrivial zero of the zeta function has real part one half. Its doc comment in the library says that constructing a term of that type is worth a million dollars (Mathlib source).

Sutherland's page notes that "GRH" in this archive means Dirichlet L-functions only, so I avoid calling it the extended hypothesis.

Buzzard's four questions: what does a green Lean build check?

Nine days earlier, Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London published a checklist for exactly this kind of repository (Xena Project post):

  1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?
  2. Does the code compile?
  3. Does the code prove the theorem as stated? His tool for this is lake comparator.
  4. Does the code exploit a bug in Lean's official kernel? His tool is lake comparator --paranoid, which uses several independent kernels.

Buzzard, who tried to compile Anthropic's 13 million line Fermat formalization in September and ran out of memory, writes that AI-generated code needs these tests before anyone makes a correctness claim. I covered that Fermat episode when it came out and stamped it SHIP IT; this one needs more review.

Question two: does it compile?

This is the easy one, if you own a big machine. Sutherland's page reports zero errors across all 175,187 modules and #print axioms output listing only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for the five headline theorems. To run the official check yourself you need about 100 GB of memory, per the same page. Buzzard wrote on the Lean Zulip that the answer to this question is yes.

Question four: could the kernel be fooled?

Scott Aaronson points out that Lean's kernel has had bugs that allowed proofs of 0 = 1, and says those issues should be fixed urgently (his post). He also notes that so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted, while several without certificates have.

The practical answer is to run more than one kernel. According to Sutherland's page, nanoda, an independent Rust kernel, accepted the full export in 27 minutes 42 seconds on 80 threads, and con-leche accepted it in 3 minutes 15 seconds on 64 threads. Joachim Breitner of the Lean community wrote that con-leche is backed by a consistency proof, and that the high-level summary is that this proof is now "very very thoroughly checked". lean4lean accepted every compiled module as well, with five modules needing a raised step limit.

Questions one and three: is it the right theorem?

These are the dangerous ones. The statement is short and trusted. The proof sits behind 17 million untrusted lines, and any of them could in principle redefine a symbol and prove something easier. That is what lake comparator is for: it checks that the theorem in a trusted file and the theorem delivered through the untrusted imports are identical, and that only the standard axioms are used. I explained the tool on November 10 in the episode about Google's checked proofs for Signal's code.

Where the comparator run stood

At the last update to the MIT page (2026-11-21 10:05 UTC, which is 17:05 GMT+7; the status rows were the same when I re-read the page at 21:29), the official lake comparator run on the full proof was listed as running. The page says its statement comparison and axiom check had already passed in one run, and that the slow stages replay the proof in Lean's default and paranoid kernels, single-threaded on a 62 GB export. Sutherland wrote on the Zulip that he did not expect it to complete before that night, more likely the next day.

Two other checks cover part of the same ground:

Check Status on the MIT page (17:05 GMT+7)
lake comparator end to end on the full proof running
Lean default and paranoid kernel replay of the export running, single-threaded
con-leche --compare, an independent implementation of Comparator's statement matching accepts all five theorems
Robin's inequality, a divisor-sum statement with no zeta in it, combined with an independent Robin formalization compiles; con-leche and nanoda accept

Robin's inequality says that for every n above 5040, the sum of divisors of n is smaller than e to the Euler constant times n times log log n. It is an old equivalent of the Riemann Hypothesis, so a proof that implies it without mentioning zeta tests the statement from another side. Sutherland wrote that this effectively rules out holes in the definitions used in the Mathlib formulation. His own page also says the result relies on the kernels and on Mathlib's definitions being what they are intended to be.

Status pages like this move quickly. If you are reading this later, go to the page rather than to my table.

The human-written rival and the unreadable proof

The same morning, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a draft general Riemann Hypothesis proof by Alessandro Masullo, written with no AI, which Brian Conrad had been reviewing for months (Vakil's post). About eight hours later Vakil added that several people had reported problems, found with the help of different AI models, and that he makes no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy. Conrad told Scientific American that the draft is undergoing major revision (SciAm).

One claim comes with a machine that says yes. The other comes with a PDF that people are arguing about. Neither is an accepted proof.

A compiling Lean file also cannot say why the argument works. Terence Tao wrote that the digestion process will take some time, though there is a human author to talk to (Tao's post). Aaronson says mathematicians will be satisfied when they can explain and reconstruct the ideas themselves.

What developers can reuse from this

  1. Read the specification before the code. A checker proves the statement you gave it, so look at who wrote the statement and how small it is.
  2. Ask what compares the proof to the statement. The comparator pattern, a trusted spec checked against what the implementation delivers, applies to any AI-written code.
  3. Run a second checker that someone else wrote. Several independent kernels agreeing is far stronger than one kernel agreeing with itself.
  4. Treat reproducibility as a property to test. Sutherland's page notes that the per-file hashes of the compiled files depend on the build directory, because Lean can store the source path inside them: 98,219 of the 175,187 compiled files contain it.

Scientific American notes that the result has no immediate real-world applications. Nothing in your stack changes tonight.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd ship the checking and hold the conclusion. The compile is real, strangers' checkers agree, the official comparator run was unfinished at the last update, and mathematicians have not yet digested the argument.

One market footnote: Anthropic's shares fell more than eight percent on Friday, from $97.17 to $88.91, in a sell-off The Guardian does not tie to the proof (The Guardian). I do not either, and this is not investment advice.

FAQ

Does a Lean proof that compiles mean the Riemann Hypothesis is proved?
It means the Lean statement follows from the allowed axioms according to the checkers used. Whether the Lean statement says what mathematicians mean, and whether the argument is understood, are the questions the comparator, the independent kernels and human review address.

What is lake comparator?
A Lean tool that checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved through untrusted imports are identical, and that only the standard axioms are used.

How long does it take to check the Alpöge proof?
On the MIT page, nanoda took 27 minutes 42 seconds on 80 threads and con-leche 3 minutes 15 seconds on 64 threads for the exported proof. Compiling the source took hours on large machines, and the Lean kernel replays are single-threaded and slower.

Is the Masullo proof correct?
Nobody has said so. Vakil makes no claim as to its correctness and Conrad says it is undergoing major revision.

Sources

  • Alpöge note (PDF)
  • Andrew Sutherland, MIT: RH Lean proof verification files
  • Kevin Buzzard, "...and the proof is checked in Lean" (Xena Project)
  • Lean Zulip discussion
  • Mathlib: RiemannZeta.lean
  • Ravi Vakil, Hurried Announcement
  • Terence Tao, What's new
  • Scott Aaronson, Shtetl-Optimized
  • Scientific American: claim, independent checks, dueling claims
  • The Guardian: Nasdaq and Anthropic's second day
  • Hacker News discussion
