articles.title: Trimming Fixed the GitHub Shape. On the Web Shape It Costs You the Answer.
articles.description: helve_dev left a comment on my trimming piece that I could not shake. He had seen the same thing in a...
articles.body_html:
helve_dev left a comment on my trimming piece that I could not shake. He had seen the same thing in a different shape: web search and extraction results, full markdown and JSON payloads, making a small model anchor on whatever was longest or loudest instead of what answered the question. Trimming to the tight fields that actually carry the answer, he said, fixed accuracy and the token bill at the same time, and it mattered most on long loops, where old results pile up over 15 or 20 turns until the model is reading boilerplate instead of facts. He had watched it happen in real traces. He had never run a clean two-sided test with scored pass rates. So I ran one. The result is not what either of us expected.

The setup is the same shape as the GitHub run, moved onto the web. Twelve questions, five pages each, all written for this test. The model searches, reads pages, and answers with the exact value: a version, a price, a flag, a limit. One arm sees the full page text in the search results. The other sees only the title, the link, and the first 200 characters of each page, and has to open a page to read the rest. Six questions hide the decisive fact inside those first 200 characters. Six hide it further down, where only opening the page finds it. Same small model as before, same six-call limit, every arm run twice. Both second runs came back identical to the first, so I am counting 24 tasks per arm, not 48.

1. The accuracy gain does not travel. It reverses.

Full pages solved 22 of 24. Trimmed pages solved 20 of 24. On the GitHub shape, trimming nearly doubled the score. On the web shape, it costs two tasks.

Both tasks it loses are the ones where the fact sits past the cut. One asks the per-seat price of a team plan after a price change. The trimmed snippet shows the cheaper plan's price first ($8, for the solo plan), and the model answers $8 and never opens the page. The real answer, $12, is three sentences further down. The other asks which command flag skips the build cache. The snippet never shows the flag, so the model opens the wrong page, the caching guide, and answers with a cache command instead. The trimmed arm solved all twelve questions where the fact was visible in the snippet, and only eight of twelve where it was not. The full arm solved all twelve of the hidden ones.

That is the shape of the failure, and it is worth naming plainly. The model does not treat a snippet as a pointer to a longer page. It treats it as the page. When the visible text contains a plausible answer (another plan's price, a related command), it answers from that and stops. Trimming only helps when the trim keeps the answer. When it cuts the answer, the model does not go looking for it. It answers with whatever the trim left behind.

2. The saving is small, and the re-open eats it

Trimmed pages cost 513 tokens per turn against 556 for full pages, and 1,472 per task against 1,667. That is 12%, not the 63% the GitHub trim saved. Two reasons. First, the pages here are short, so the gap between a full result and a trimmed one is only about 70 tokens. Second, the trimmed arm opens pages more often (0.67 opens per task against 0.42), and every open drops a full page into the history. By the third turn, the trimmed arm's prompt is actually bigger than the full arm's: 791 tokens against 783. The saving exists on the first turn and is gone by the third.

This is the part helve_dev's traces got right and my test sharpens. The bill on a long loop is not set by the size of one result. It is set by what stays in the history. Every result the model sees stays there, turn after turn, and every page it opens to recover a trimmed fact stays there too. Trimming one result does not trim the history. It just moves tokens from the search result into the re-open.

3. Both arms balloon the same way

Turn one costs about 162 tokens in both arms. Turn two costs 722 for full pages and 651 for trimmed. Turn three costs 783 and 791. That is nearly a fivefold rise in three turns, whatever the payload size, because the history only grows. The trim does not bend the curve. It shifts it by one turn at most.

The honest limit here is that nothing in this test ran long. Every task ended in three turns, so the 15-to-20-turn loops helve_dev described never happened. The curve to turn three is real evidence; the curve to turn twenty is still his traces, not my numbers. But the direction of the evidence is against the trim: if the history grows fivefold in three turns in both arms, a longer loop does not fix that by trimming harder. It makes the re-opens pile up faster.

4. The two arms fail in opposite ways

The full arm's only failure is a question needing two facts, a version and a date. It answered the date and dropped the version. The trimmed arm solved that one, and all three two-fact questions. Short results seem to help the model hold two facts at once. That is three tasks, and I will not lean on it. But the pattern is neat enough to note: full pages cost you the second fact, trimmed pages cost you the hidden fact. Neither shape is free. The question is which fact your task hides.

So where does that leave helve_dev's claim? Half right, in a way that matters. Trimming does cut the bill on the web shape, a little, not a lot, and only until the model starts re-opening pages. And trimming does not fix accuracy here. It breaks it, exactly on the questions where the answer sits past the cut. The GitHub trim worked because every decisive fact sat inside the first 300 characters by design. The web does not promise that. A page puts the price of the wrong plan first and the right one third. A snippet is not a summary. It is the top of a page, and the top of a page is where the least important facts live.

The fix I am keeping is narrower than the one I went in with. Trim the search result, yes, but only when the snippet is built to carry the answer, not just the first 200 characters of whatever the page happens to start with. And if the answer might sit past the cut, the model needs a reason to open the page before it answers, not permission to. A snippet that shows a plausible wrong answer is worse than no snippet at all, because the model will take it and stop.

Have you watched a small model answer from a snippet instead of opening the page? What made it open the page — a better snippet, a different instruction, or just a bigger model? I am curious what worked, because trimming alone did not.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Mingle (MIT): Bring Your Local Coding Agents into Slack, Discord, Telegram & More — With Zero Servers
articles.description: Bringing your own coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, etc.) into custom...
articles.body_html:
Bringing your own coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, etc.) into custom tooling is pretty common now. What still bothered me about most agent-to-IM bridges was the cloud relay: if a third-party server sits between your chat apps and your agent, your private work conversations pass through someone else's infrastructure—bringing both the risk of a server breach and the risk of your data being logged or sold.

So I built Mingle (MIT-licensed)—a zero-server desktop app that lets you bring your local coding agents directly into the chat apps you already use: Slack, Discord, Telegram, iMessage, WeChat, Feishu/Lark, WeCom, DingTalk, QQ, and GitHub Issues/PRs.

Why zero-server matters

Mingle has no backend service at all:

  • No Mingle server, no accounts, no telemetry.
  • Direct platform connections: connects straight to each chat platform's official bot interface (or your local Apple ID for iMessage)—never routed through a hosted Mingle relay.
  • Localhost-only surface: the local console and API bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
  • OS keychain for secrets: bot tokens and credentials stay inside macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI, or Linux Secret Service.
  • Plain-file memory: each agent's persona and memory are ordinary files in a local folder (ROLE.md, MEMORY.md, and notes/).
  • Optional 24/7 mode on your own hardware: if you want your agent online when your laptop sleeps, you can deploy the runtime to your own SSH host directly from the app—still your machine, no middleman.

What makes it usable in real chats

Connecting a CLI agent to a webhook is easy to demo; making it behave well in daily group chats took most of the real engineering:

  1. One agent, unified memory across chat apps The same agent can join your Slack workspace, Discord server, and Telegram/WeChat groups while sharing one continuous memory. You can ask it in one app what was decided in another, or ask it to forward a summary across platforms.
  2. Parallel side tasks without blocking chat When you hand it heavy work—writing code, investigating a bug, running long shell commands—it forks the work into a background task (opening native threads in Slack, Discord, and Feishu) while staying responsive in the main room.
  3. Group-chat etiquette It listens passively, responds when addressed by name or nickname without needing an @ on every message, and automatically throttles itself in busy channels instead of spamming every turn.
  4. 14 coding-agent harnesses + one-click session handoff Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Kimi Code, Cursor, and 9 more harnesses via OAR. You can also hand off an existing session's context and preferences into a Mingle agent in one click.

Honest current status

Mingle started about a week ago and is currently at v0.4.8—definitely early:

  • End-to-end verified harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Kimi Code.
  • Chat platforms: Feishu is battle-tested on a live tenant; the other connectors are currently verified against platform APIs and automated tests.
  • Installers: macOS (Apple-signed & notarized), Windows (unsigned for now), Linux, plus a one-line install script.

Links

  • GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/earayu/Mingle
  • Website & docs: https://mingle.build

If you try it out, I'd love feedback on the zero-server architecture, the SSH deployment flow, or any quirks you hit with a specific chat platform—feel free to drop a comment here or open an issue on GitHub.

articles.title: The Provider Said 'Already Charged'. Nothing Was Charged.
articles.description: Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book...
articles.body_html:
Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book twice, and twice my site told her she had already paid. Her bank showed nothing, and no order existed on my side. She asked whether I had taken her money and forgotten the book. I had not taken anything. My checkout had refused her money and then told her the refusal was her own history.

That email is the whole piece. A provider saying "already charged" is a rumour, not a receipt, and most payment code treats it as a verdict. It should not. On a first attempt the provider's word can be wrong in the direction nobody checks for: it can say the money moved when nothing moved at all. If your code believes it, you do something quieter than double-charging anyone. You turn away a customer who is trying to pay you, and no statement, no dashboard, no alert ever shows you did it.

ilragioniere put this to me in the comments, and he put it better than I could. He called it the false positive, and the quietest failure in the whole series: a provider that answers "already charged" when nothing was charged skips a real charge forever, and no statement ever shows it. His floor under it: the provider's own settlement report, a charge record nobody prunes, dated, independent of the key. Inside the lag, answer "unknown, hold" and let the file settle it when it lands. So I ran his shape. I built a small stand-in for the provider, one that lies on purpose, and I put two ways of handling a first attempt through the same 10 tries, twice over.

The stand-in answers "already charged" on every first attempt, even when no charge exists and no settlement line exists. That is the lie, stated plainly. The first handler is the three-line version: if the provider says already charged, skip. It never looks at the settlement file. The second handler reads the provider's answer and refuses to trust it. It says "unknown, hold", waits for the settlement file to land, and reads that instead. No line in the file means no settlement, and the charge goes ahead. A matching line means the charge is real, and nothing is charged twice.

The count is what makes this more than an opinion. Across 60 first attempts the stand-in said "already charged" 60 times, and in all 60 nothing had been charged. The trusting handler skipped 20 out of 20 real charges, $580 of payments refused, and never once looked at the file. The careful handler charged 20 out of 20 when the file held no matching line, $580 taken properly, and recognised the charge 20 out of 20 times when the file did hold one, with zero second charges. Same lie, same tries. The only difference was what each handler treated as evidence.

Five things I took away from that count.

  1. The lie leaves no trace. A double charge is loud. The customer sees $58 for a $29 book and asks for a refund. A skipped charge is silent. The provider took nothing, the file lists nothing, and the only record of the missing money is a customer deciding whether to write in or just leave. Ana wrote in. Most people do not; they assume the site is broken and buy the book somewhere else. Your numbers stay clean while sales quietly shrink, and nothing in your records can tell you why.

  2. The two mistakes are not the same size. A false "not charged" costs a double charge, a refund, and a thread with an unhappy customer. Somebody sees it the same day. A false "already charged" costs one charge nobody sees, found only if a customer complains. The loud error gets the guardrails and the late-night fixes. The quiet one gets trusted code and a shrug, because nobody has felt it yet. That is exactly backwards. The error you cannot see is the one you have to design against, not the one you will notice.

  3. The key cannot rescue this one. The key is a good tool for the job it does. If the charge landed and your own record of it did not, the key stops the retry from charging twice. But this failure happens before any of that. It is a first attempt. Nothing was charged, so there is no key entry worth asking about, and if the key was pruned it is gone anyway. A key proves a retry is the same request. It was never a receipt.

  4. The search lags, and the lag has a floor. The other place people look is the charge search: ask by your own order number instead of by key. It beats the key, and the previous piece showed it surviving a pruned key. But a search is not a read. It lags the charge by seconds, and inside those seconds the only honest answer is that you do not know yet. Code that cannot say "I don't know" fills the gap with whatever answer arrives first, usually the provider's confident one. The floor under the lag is the file: the settlement report lands on its own schedule, dated, and once it lands it does not change its mind.

  5. The file is the only thing nobody prunes. Keys get pruned, searches lag. The settlement file is the provider's own record of money that actually moved, written down after the fact, and it answers a different question from the other two: not "do you remember this request" but "did this money move". With the line absent, the careful handler's answer was not "already charged" but "no settlement", with the age of the attempt attached, and then it charged. With the line present, it said charged, and it was right. It is not fast or convenient. It is the one record that does not depend on the answer you are trying to check.

There is a limit to what this run can claim, and I would rather state it plainly. The provider here is a stand-in I built, not a real payment company, and the settlement file is one I wrote myself, landing a second after each attempt. The shape of the lie is real and the counts are real, but a real provider's file could arrive late, mangled, or not at all, and I did not measure that. The check that would close this properly needs a real sandbox account, a real charge, a pruned key, and both answers held up against the settlement line. I have not done that one, and I am not going to pretend the stand-in is the same thing. What it does prove is narrower: the three-line shortcut fails every time the provider is wrong, and the hold-and-read shape survives the same lie in both directions, twenty times out of twenty.

So here is where I land. Never let a provider's "already charged" be the last word on whether money moved. Read it, then check the record that does not depend on it. Inside the lag, say you do not know, wait for the file, and let the file decide. It costs a second and one extra read per attempt. The alternative costs customers you will never hear from, which is a strange price to pay for saving a second.

Has this one bitten you? As a buyer, were you ever told you had already paid when your bank said otherwise, and what did you do, write in or walk away? As a builder, what do you check first when a charge is in doubt, the provider's answer or your own records, and has the provider's answer ever been wrong for you? Tell me what you found. The quiet failures are the ones I only hear about when somebody says so out loud.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Interaction Nets Explained: The Programming Model Behind the Frostbite CPU
articles.description: On November 18, 2026, the chip-design startup Architect Labs published a post introducing Frostbite....
articles.body_html:
On November 18, 2026, the chip-design startup Architect Labs published a post introducing Frostbite. They describe it as a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set. They say their AI systems designed it, from the compiler down to the final chip layout. The Hacker News thread reached 657 points and 342 comments.

Most coverage is about the AI and the headline number: 4.59x better performance per watt than a conventional core. This article looks at the part software developers can try today. Frostbite runs programs as interaction nets, a model of computation that is more than 35 years old. The language that compiles to it, Vine, is open source, and you can install it with Cargo today.

A note on sources: I have not run Vine or seen Frostbite hardware. Every number below comes from the linked sources: the Frostbite post, the Vine documentation, an explainer from the company behind Vine, and the HN discussion.

What Frostbite claims, in short

All of these come from the Architect Labs post:

  • The workloads. 25 programs in five groups: parallel, staged, sequential, branching, and recursive. The agents tuned the design on 10 of them. The other 15 were held out until the final evaluation.
  • The headline result. One Frostbite "quad" (a two-by-two group of tiles) reached a geometric mean of 4.59x the performance per watt of the comparison core across all 25 workloads. That splits into 6.02x on the 10 tuning workloads and 3.83x on the 15 held-out ones.
  • Area. An average 8.77x performance per area, on a 7 nm process.
  • The baseline. The comparison core is "a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core". A footnote says: "For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU."
  • The status. The design reached 500 MHz in the final GDS (the layout file sent to a chip factory). The post itself calls the power numbers "pre-silicon". It does not report results from a manufactured chip.
  • The process. The specification ended as formal contracts that compiled to more than 800,000 lines of Lean (a proof assistant). The agents tried 58 design ideas and kept 37.

Why can this design drop so much of a normal CPU's hardware? The answer is in the programming model.

Why your CPU spends energy guessing

A normal compiler sees which operations in your program depend on each other. It uses that information for optimization. Then it throws most of it away and produces one long list of instructions.

The CPU then tries to rebuild that information at runtime. Out-of-order cores keep large buffers to find instructions that can run early. Multicore chips add cache coherence protocols so every core sees the same memory, because any instruction might touch any address.

The explainer from Tendrils, the company that develops Vine, puts it this way: "Normal compilers already track these dependencies internally and use them to make optimizations. However, this information is then thrown away and the entire program is linearized into a sequence of instructions."

Frostbite's post shows the cost. Leaving out clock distribution, the comparison core spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Only 13% goes to computing. Interaction nets keep the dependency information instead.

Interaction nets in four ideas

Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont in a 1990 paper at POPL, a major programming-languages conference. The model fits in four ideas.

1. A program is a graph of nodes. Each node has exactly one principal port (its main connection point) and zero or more auxiliary ports (extra connection points). Wires connect ports. In the simple examples, a number and an addition are both nodes.

2. Computation is rewriting pairs. When a wire connects the principal ports of two nodes, they form an active pair. A rule says how that pair is replaced by a small new piece of graph. Then the next active pair is rewritten, and so on, until none are left. Each step only touches the two nodes involved. Tendrils calls this property locality.

3. Active pairs never overlap. A node has only one principal port, so it can be part of only one active pair at a time. That means all active pairs are independent. You can rewrite them in any order, or all at once, and the final result is the same. This property is called confluence. In practice it means no race conditions: there is no shared variable for two threads to fight over.

4. Every value is used exactly once. This is linearity. If a value needs to be used twice, the net contains an explicit duplicate node. If it is not used, an explicit erase node destroys it. Nothing is copied or dropped by accident. Rust developers will recognize the idea: it is close to ownership.

The Tendrils explainer shows this with unary arithmetic. In its multiplication example, the first rewrite leaves two independent active pairs, which can run in parallel with no coordination. Nobody added that parallelism. It is a side effect of keeping the dependencies.

What linearity looks like in Vine

Nobody wants to wire graph nodes by hand. Vine is a language with syntax close to Rust that compiles to interaction nets. Its Apache-2.0 GitHub repository calls it "an experimental new programming language based on interaction nets". Vine compiles to Ivy, a low-level net language, which runs on a runtime called the IVM. The Frostbite post says programs for the chip are written in Vine and compiled to Ivy.

Linearity shows up in Vine's type system as "flexibility". The Fork and Drop documentation says every type has two yes-or-no properties: can its values be forked (copied), and can they be dropped (destroyed)? The annotations work like regex quantifiers:

  • No annotation: values must be used exactly once.
  • ?: values may be used zero or one times (droppable).
  • +: values may be used one or more times (forkable).
  • *: values may be used zero or more times (both).

When you use a variable twice, the compiler inserts a fork for you. The docs show (used_multiple_times, used_multiple_times) becoming (used_multiple_times.fork(), used_multiple_times) behind the scenes.

The IO type cannot be forked or dropped. The docs explain the result: "at any point in the execution of a Vine program, there is exactly one IO handle, so all IO operations are ordered." So the language gets ordered side effects from the type system, while pure computation stays free to run in parallel.

Measure your program's parallelism with one flag

Vine can tell you how parallel a program is, without any parallel hardware.

The installation page needs Rust and one command:

cargo install --git https://github.com/VineLang/vine --locked

Every Vine program needs a main function that takes the IO handle. The hello world is:

pub fn main(&io: &IO) {
  io.println("Hello, world!");
}

Run it with vine run hello_world.vi. After the output, Vine prints statistics. The docs show 341 total interactions for this program. The statistics page says the total interaction count is deterministic: "the same program will always have the exact same interaction count, no matter what machine it is run on." That makes it a stable measure of work, unlike wall-clock time.

The useful flag is --breadth-first. The CLI docs say it runs the program so that "at each step, every possible interaction is performed in parallel." This pretends you have a machine with unlimited cores. It reports three numbers:

  • Total: all interactions, the amount of work.
  • Depth: the number of parallel steps needed. This is the critical path, the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another.
  • Breadth: total divided by depth, the average number of interactions ready at each step.

This is the work-span model from algorithms courses: total is the work, depth is the span, and breadth is the average parallelism.

A worked example: longest common subsequence

The Tendrils explainer uses the longest common subsequence problem. Given two lists, find the length of the longest sequence of items that appears in both, in order, but not always next to each other. For "Tendrils" and "edits", the answer is "edis", length 4.

Here is their Vine code, a plain dynamic-programming version with two nested loops and no parallel hints:

pub fn lcs[T*; Eq[T]](a: List[T], b: List[T]) -> N32 {
  let row = [];
  for a_elem in a {
    let prev_row_entry = 0;
    let prev_new_entry = 0;
    let new_row = [];
    for b_elem in b {
      let row_entry = row.pop_front().or_use(0);
      let new_entry = if a_elem == b_elem {
        prev_row_entry + 1
      } else {
        row_entry.max(prev_new_entry)
      };
      prev_row_entry = row_entry;
      prev_new_entry = new_entry;
      new_row.push_back(new_entry);
    }
    row = new_row;
  }

  row.get(b.len() - 1).or_use(0)
}

Note the T* in the signature. With the flexibility rules above, that says list items may be copied or dropped freely.

They ran it on two random lists of 200 items with vine run lcs.vi --breadth-first:

Interactions
  Total            2_993_893
    Depth             10_920
    Breadth              274

On average, 274 interactions could run at each step. Then they increased both lists to 2,000 items:

Interactions
  Total          296_223_905
    Depth            108_142
    Breadth            2_739

The total work grew about 100x, because the algorithm is quadratic. The depth grew only about 10x. The explainer gives the reason: every cell on a diagonal of the DP table is independent of the others, so the critical path is just the main diagonal, which grows linearly. The parallel work grows with the input.

The explainer says the Vine compiler does this "not by magically extracting parallelism out of the program; it simply preserves dependency information all the way down to the hardware (or runtime, in this case)."

Frostbite's post shows the same pattern on a smaller problem. For five queens on a five-by-five board, the net runs 3,183 interactions with a critical path of 262 steps. On average, about twelve interactions are ready at every step.

How to read your own numbers

If you try this on your own algorithms, keep two limits in mind:

  • Breadth-first mode is optimistic. The CLI docs say it "gives an upper bound on the speedup that could be seen from a parallel machine." Real hardware has a fixed number of cores and pays to move work between them.
  • Depth is the floor. No hardware can finish faster than the critical path. A program with a breadth near 1 is sequential, whatever the chip is. This is close to Amdahl's law, and one HN commenter made that point about general-purpose code: "the longest serial task is what ends up slowing everything down."

From a net to a chip: how Frostbite schedules work

Frostbite is a grid of tiles. Each tile has a small local memory, an engine, and a runtime block. Because every value has one owner and every step is local, data can sit in small memories next to where it is used, instead of in a deep shared cache.

There is no central scheduler. The Frostbite post says each tile follows three rules:

  1. Run your own work first (the work in your input ports).
  2. If you have none, take work from a neighboring tile that has some to spare.
  3. If no neighbor has any, go inactive and save power.

Per the post, when a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces, the running code parks what comes next in a small record (the "frame manager"), puts the new tasks on a hardware "work queue", and takes the newest one itself. Idle neighbors pull the rest over the on-chip network. When the last piece returns, the parked code wakes up.

The post calls this "stealing work". Java developers know the same idea from ForkJoinPool, which its docs describe as "employing work-stealing". Here it is built into the tile hardware. The post says no human specified it and that it can be traced to "necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics."

The energy breakdown shows the trade. A Frostbite quad cuts memory energy to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on the on-chip network and scheduler. Frostbite moves energy from guessing about dependencies to moving messages between tiles.

What the numbers do not show yet

The baseline is a small core, and it is not named. A dual-issue, in-order core is far simpler than the out-of-order cores in laptops and servers. One HN commenter pointed this out: "Actual modern high-performance CPUs use way larger than dual-issue front-ends." The post says comparisons against larger out-of-order CPUs, multicore setups, and the SPEC and PARSEC benchmark suites are planned "in the coming months".

The power numbers are pre-silicon. They come from models and RTL (hardware description code), not a measured chip. The post says they can be matched to real chips "over multiple tapeout loops", which has not happened yet.

The held-out score is the one to quote. The post reports both 6.02x on tuning workloads and 3.83x on held-out ones. When someone repeats "4.59x", remember that 3.83x is the number for programs the design never saw.

The workloads are small. Three kernels follow the SPLASH-2 suite but are "64 times smaller", per the post. Another HN commenter noted that the tests are compute-heavy kernels on small working sets, and asked how the design handles programs that "build large data structures and slowly mutate them."

Debugging changes. A commenter pointed out that there is no call stack or program counter, and that nets can leak values or get stuck waiting on each other. Vine's own statistics page touches on this: the Allocated and Freed memory numbers should always match, and "if they differ, that indicates that there was a vicious circle in the interaction net." Vine has a debug mode, but the same commenter called a source-level debugger "a requirement" and said that building one, if it does not exist yet, "would represent a substantial engineering project."

Some framing is disputed. The Frostbite post and the Tendrils explainer both say single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s; one commenter disagreed, citing yearly gains in Apple's chips. Another argued that the ideas came from decades of human research, and the AI turned them into an engineered product.

Who builds what

Two companies appear in this story. Architect Labs built Frostbite; its launch post mentions "$24M in seed funding led by Kindred Ventures". Tendrils develops Vine; its November 10 announcement says it raised $30M in a round led by Benchmark to build its own processor "to have thousands of cores operating in parallel."

The Frostbite post cites Vine and the Tendrils explainer. An HN commenter asked whether the two companies are related. Neither post says, so treat them as separate projects that share a language.

The Frostbite post lists its next steps: an FPGA-hosted playground where anyone can run programs, a basic operating system, benchmarks against a broader set of CPUs, and a release of the RTL and ISA.

What you can do with this today

  • Run your algorithms with --breadth-first. Depth and breadth show how much of your code is a serial chain and how much is independent work. If a rewrite lowers depth, it has more room for parallel speedup on any machine.
  • Notice where you share mutable state. Interaction nets make every copy and drop explicit. Asking "who owns this value?" in Java, Go, or Rust is the same habit that makes concurrent code safer.
  • Watch for the FPGA playground and the SPEC results. They will show whether the 3.83x held-out number survives real hardware and stronger baselines.

Frostbite may or may not become a product. The model under it is well defined and available now in a language you can install with one command.

Would you write code for a chip with no program counter and no shared memory, if the tooling caught leaks and stuck nets for you?

Sources

  • [1] Introducing Frostbite, Architect Labs
  • [2] Hacker News discussion of Frostbite
  • [3] On Interaction Nets, Tendrils
  • [4] Interaction nets, Wikipedia (cites Lafont, POPL 1990)
  • [5] Vine documentation
  • [6] Vine on GitHub
  • [7] Vine docs: Fork and Drop
  • [8] Vine docs: Using the CLI
  • [9] Vine docs: Statistics
  • [10] Introducing Architect Labs
  • [11] Tendrils: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU

articles.title: Meet BetterZoom: the only self diagnostic app with smart rowdy intelligence needed
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge             What I Built   For...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge
 

What I Built

For the SmartSpectra SDK Challenge, I built an app that might make Zoom, google meet obsolete forever considering the office meetings are highly unproductive due to managers fail to keep tabs on their juniors/team members & ultimately failing to track their emotional/mental state; results in dead productivity. My app features 2 modes: self mode which is uniquly built to train/regulate your ownself for tough situations. The next feature is main highlight (Meetings) which would allow a host to combine the power of SDK monitoring with use Artifical Intelligence to be much more aware about their team mates.

Meeting Mode (main highlight)

The problem

  • Meetings eat up a huge share of the working day, and most people think they don't work. In a Harvard Business School survey of 182 senior managers, 71% said meetings are unproductive and inefficient, and 65% said meetings keep them from finishing their own work.
  • In Atlassian's 2024 State of Teams survey of 5,000 knowledge workers, 78% said they struggle to get their work done because of how many meetings they have.
  • A big reason: the host can't watch everyone at once. With 5 other faces on screen, it's easy to miss who has switched off, who is nervous to speak, or who is overwhelmed. The meeting slowly loses its purpose.

What BetterZoom does about it

  • Every participant who agrees is measured on their own laptop: pulse, breathing, HRV and face signals (looking at the screen, talking, blinking, expressions).
  • The host sees a live one-word state next to each person's video, updated every second: Calm, Steady, Tense or Anxious. No charts, no clutter, unless the host wants them.
  • Every 25 seconds, a small summary of numbers (never video) goes to the host. It covers attention, talking time, expressions and heart rhythm.
  • The host taps the bot on someone's card, and Smokey writes a 3–4 line summary in seconds: how that person seems now, what changed over the meeting, and a gentle suggestion like "invite their thoughts" or "give them a moment." He can read it out loud.
  • One tap for the full picture: a report window with trend charts for pulse, breathing and HRV, attention signals and expressions.
  • Before leaving, the host can download a .md report card for every participant, or a CSV of all readings.

Built on consent, not surveillance

  • Nobody is measured unless they say yes. Everyone sees a "Reporting to host" badge on anyone who is sharing, and anyone can stop with one click.
  • The AI only ever sees "P1, P2…", never names or video. Everything is wiped when the host leaves the meeting.

In numbers: up to 6 people per meeting · live state every 1 s · reports every 25 s · AI summary on demand in 3–4 lines · 0 videos uploaded or stored.

Self Mode

  • Built for emotional and mental regulation for tense situation preparation: Job interviews, Public speaking, or Startup Pitches. Even managers can use this feature to prep before hoping on a call or briefing about something important to their bosses.

  • Monitors your facial expression, registers your emotional state and uses Smart Intelligence system (Smokey Bot referrence in the video) to help you navigate through the situation.

  • Smokey turns your signals into coaching. Every 30 seconds he gets a snapshot of your pulse, breathing rate, HRV, calm level and expressions, compared with your own normal. He also knows what you're practising for.

  • He reads the patterns. Fast breathing and a rising pulse usually mean nerves, which is common in a job interview. He spots that and gives you a quick fix, like "inhale for four seconds, exhale for six" or "drop your shoulders and pause before answering." Calm numbers? He tells you to keep that pace.

  • A real example: in one of my runs my breathing jumped to about 30 breaths a minute while I talked. Smokey caught it within half a minute and walked me through slowing it down.

 

Demo


 

Code

Github Repo: https://github.com/Msohaib-maker/SneakMeet

Note: My Github repo includes all the necessary intructions to install & use the Windows App.

How It Responds to Human Signals

We have SDK integrated in both of our app modules: self mode and Group Mode. The SDK provides us the following readings:

Reading What it means
Pulse Compared with your own resting pulse, not an average person's. "↑ a bit higher than usual" means something.
Breathing rate The strongest sign of nerves in my testing. Fast breathing pushes the calm meter towards Tense.
HRV (plus average beat gap, SDNN and stress index) Shown once you've sat still for about a minute. Higher variability usually means more relaxed.
Breathing waveforms (chest and belly) Drawn live, and used to tell whether you breathe mostly from your chest or your belly.
Pulse waveform Drawn live, one peak per heartbeat.
Expressions, blinking, talking Your main expression appears as a meme-style sticker on your video. Talking tells the app to ignore breathing for a moment, because speech throws breathing readings off.

How the experience reacts in real time

Self mode (practising for an interview, pitch or talk):

  1. For the first ~30 seconds the app quietly learns your normal pulse and breathing.
  2. After that, a calm meter (Calm → Steady → Tense → Anxious) moves as your body reacts, with the reason shown underneath: "Pulse 86, 8 above your baseline."
  3. Every 30 seconds the numbers go to Gemini, and Smokey (my AI host) answers in character and out loud. In one of my runs my breathing climbed to around 30 breaths a minute while I talked. Smokey noticed and told me: "Slow your breathing right down by inhaling for four seconds and exhaling for six."
  4. At the end you get a debrief: how your calm level changed over the session, strengths, things to work on, and a downloadable report.

Meeting mode:

  1. Participants who agree to share get a live one-word state next to their video: Calm, Steady, Tense or Anxious. Only the host sees it.
  2. Every 25 seconds a small summary (numbers only) goes to the host.
  3. The host taps the little bot on someone's card, and Gemini writes a 3–4 line summary of how that person seems and what changed. Smokey can read it out.

How I integrated the SDK

  • BetterZoom is an Electron desktop app using @smartspectra/node-sdk. The same camera stream feeds both the video call and the SDK (useMediaStream), so nobody needs two cameras.
  • I request three groups of readings: breathing (rate plus chest/belly traces), heart (pulse, pressure waveform, HRV) and face (blinks, talking, expressions). The SDK sends roughly 28 updates a second, which I decode with decodeMetrics.
  • I only trust readings the SDK is confident about: below 45% for pulse or 40% for breathing, the app shows the number faded with a "weak signal" label instead of guessing.
  • The SDK's camera checks (face too low, chest not visible, frame rate too low) appear on screen as plain tips, so people can fix their setup themselves.
  • The calm meter is my own logic on top of the SDK. It compares pulse and breathing with your personal baseline, smooths them out, and ignores breathing while you talk.

My honest experience

After about 90 credits of testing:

  • Expressions and breathing came through well. Most of the time the SDK reported around 68–73% confidence for me, and the readings matched how I actually felt.
  • Pulse usually appears after 15–25 seconds. I'm not a medical expert, so I can't judge how accurate it is, but it stayed in a believable range and reacted when I got nervous.
  • Expressions are not perfect. The SDK sometimes read me as neutral or sad when I was actually tense.
  • Breathing needs your chest in view, and HRV needs about a minute of sitting still. That's rare while you're talking, so HRV often didn't show up during practice.
  • Frame rate is the big one. The SDK needs 25+ fps and stops itself if the camera can't keep up. At first my app was the problem: redrawing the screen on every update and animating Smokey starved the SDK, and it stopped after about 15 seconds. Throttling the UI, freezing animations while measuring, and sending lighter video in meetings took my runs from stopping early to 5 minutes without a break. Dim rooms and power-saving laptops can still cause it, because webcams lower their frame rate in bad light.
  • Some readings listed in the SDK (breathing amplitude, apnea, inhale/exhale ratio) aren't available yet. Requesting them makes the SDK refuse to start, so I left them out.

The 68–73% figure and the expression observations are yours, so I've kept them as your experience. Everything else comes from the logs of our test runs.

Prize Categories

I am going to say I would personally put my app in Thoughful Category with a bit of creativity. Office meetings as I mentioned earlier woul have been the best use case for my application given the API has high amount of credits. Given SDK can be used to monitor particpants' expressions and state of comfort would help the team managers/HRs to be better decision makers. We might be looking forward to see many people never mad to be part of meetings because of their state of comfort or we could be looking to companies adapting to new meet policies which ultimately get them better meet profits.

Consent and Data Handling

Camera consent

  • BetterZoom only uses your camera and microphone after Windows asks for your permission. No other page or website can use them.
  • Readings are off until you start them yourself: by pressing Practice solo, Measure vitals or Start scan.
  • In meetings, nothing is shared by default. When a meeting has a host, every participant sees a consent popup first. It names the host and explains what will be measured, what is sent, how often, and that an AI may summarise it. You can say no and still stay in the meeting.
  • While someone is sharing, everyone in the meeting sees a "Reporting to host" badge on their video. They can stop at any time with one click. There is no hidden or background monitoring.

What is measured and where it goes

  • All readings (pulse, breathing, HRV, waveforms, face signals and expressions) are calculated on your own computer by the SmartSpectra SDK. Video frames are never uploaded or recorded.
  • Self mode: your readings stay on your laptop. Only numbers go to the AI (see below).
  • Meetings: video and audio go directly between participants (peer-to-peer, encrypted by WebRTC). A participant's readings go only to the host, and only if they agreed: a short update every second, plus a summary every 25 seconds. These are numbers only, never images.
  • Our server (on Fly.io) helps people connect and passes AI requests on to Gemini. It never sees video and stores nothing.

AI (Google Gemini)

  • Smokey's coaching and summaries are written by Google Gemini. The app sends only numbers (pulse, breathing, calm level, expression scores), never video.
  • In meetings, participants are sent as P1, P2…, never by name. The real name is added back on the host's computer.
  • On Gemini's free tier, Google may use this data to improve its products. The consent popup says so.
  • Smokey's voice uses the voices built into Windows, which work offline. No audio is sent anywhere.

Storage, retention and deletion

  • Nothing is stored on a server. In meetings, reports and AI summaries live only in the host's app memory and are deleted when the host leaves the meeting or closes the app.
  • Files (the Self mode debrief, report cards, CSV) are saved only if you click download. They are then your files to keep or delete.
  • The app keeps only your settings on your computer. Uninstalling the app removes them.

SDK telemetry

  • The SmartSpectra SDK signs in to Presage with an API key, which lives on our server and is handed to the app when measuring starts. It also sends session telemetry by default; see Presage's Telemetry and Privacy (https://smartspectra.presagetech.com/docs/telemetry-and-privacy) page.

Not medical

  • All values are wellness estimates. BetterZoom is not a medical device, makes no diagnosis, and must not be used for medical decisions. Labels like "Calm" or "Tense" are estimates from camera readings, not facts about how someone feels.

Looking forwars to the results for SmartSpectra SDK challenge.

Still reaching for Redux every time you need to manage state in a React application?

There's a simpler approach worth learning: Zustand.

Zustand is a lightweight state management library for React that makes it easy to share and update state without a lot of boilerplate. And if you'd like to learn it hands-on, I'm making my popular Getting Started with Zustand course available with lifetime FREE access 🎉

Why Learn Zustand?

As React applications grow, managing shared state across components can become challenging. Zustand offers a straightforward way to create stores, access state, update it, and organize state management logic.

In this practical course, you'll learn the fundamentals and apply them to real applications—not just isolated examples.

📚 What You'll Learn

🧠 Zustand fundamentals: Stores, selectors, middleware, DevTools and asynchronous actions.
🌐 API integration: Manage state while working with API calls and asynchronous data.
🔄 Immutable state updates: Update objects, arrays and nested state; learn how Immer can help.
🧰 Custom hooks and debugging: Organize and troubleshoot your state management code.
💾 Persistence: Explore practical persistence scenarios, including shopping cart state.

Build a user management app with CRUD operations using:

🔗 View the live demo

You'll see how to organize state and use Zustand in a practical application.

🔗 View the live demo

You'll apply Zustand to a familiar application scenario and work with state across multiple components and features.

💪 Put Your Learning Into Practice

The course also includes an additional project challenge to help you apply the concepts independently.

You'll receive the complete course and project source code, so you can follow along, review the code, and revisit the implementations whenever you need to.

I've had the opportunity to teach and mentor 3000+ developers over the years. Making this course free is my small way of giving back to the developer community and helping more people access practical, project-based learning.

I hope it helps you build your skills, strengthen your React knowledge, and discover a simpler way to manage state in your applications.

articles.title: TypeScript 7 Is \"10x Faster\". I Measured It on a Real Project
articles.description: TypeScript 7 is the compiler rewritten in Go, and Microsoft says it's about 10× faster. So I tested...
articles.body_html:
TypeScript 7 is the compiler rewritten in Go, and Microsoft says it's about 10× faster. So I tested it: the same real project on the same Mac, TypeScript 6 versus 7. Here are the numbers, how to upgrade, and the one thing that broke.

Video version:

What changed

  • The compiler was ported from TypeScript to Go. Before, tsc was JavaScript running on Node; now it's native code that type-checks on multiple threads.
  • It's still the same typescript npm package and the same tsc command.
  • The language didn't change. Your types mean the same thing.
  • TypeScript 6.0 was the last JavaScript-based version, a bridge release that deprecated the options 7.0 removes.

The test

  • Project: Hono, a popular web framework known for heavy, complex types. I used two of its configs: tsconfig.build.json (source only) and tsconfig.spec.json (source + tests, 908 files loaded).
  • Machine: Apple M4, 24 GB RAM.
  • Versions: typescript@6.0.3 vs typescript@7.0.2, installed side by side.
  • Method: tsc -p <config> --noEmit. Hono uses composite builds, so I deleted every .tsbuildinfo before each run to keep runs cold. Five runs each; I report the median. Memory is the peak resident size from /usr/bin/time -l. 
find . -name '*.tsbuildinfo' -not -path './node_modules/*' -delete
/usr/bin/time -l ../ts6/node_modules/.bin/tsc -p tsconfig.spec.json --noEmit

The results

TS 6.0.3 TS 7.0.2 Speedup
Source only 1.44 s 0.28 s 5.1×
Source + tests 4.39 s 0.69 s 6.4×
Peak memory (source + tests) 890 MB 758 MB 15% less
TS 7 with --singleThreaded 1.17 s 3.7×

The raw runs for source + tests: TS 6 took 4.58, 4.36, 4.39, 4.34 and 4.53 s; TS 7 took 0.68, 0.74, 0.69, 0.72 and 0.69 s.

So it's not quite 10× on this project, but 6.4× is huge. Even with multi-threading turned off (--singleThreaded), TS 7 was 3.7× faster, just from being native code. Your speedup depends on the project's size, its types and your CPU cores. Bigger projects and slower CI machines usually gain more.

--extendedDiagnostics showed where the time goes. TS 6 spent 3.61 s of its 4.28 s in the checker; TS 7 did the same check in 0.57 s.

How to upgrade 

npm install -D typescript@7
npx tsc -v          # Version 7.0.2
npx tsc --noEmit    # same command as before

Your tsconfig.json stays the same, as long as you've fixed the deprecation warnings from TypeScript 6. Options deprecated in 6.0 are removed in 7.0. Upgrade to 6 first, fix the warnings, then move to 7.

What broke: the same error, on a different line

TypeScript 6 type-checked Hono's tests with 0 errors. TypeScript 7 found 4:

src/hono.test.ts(3522,3): error TS2578: Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive.
src/hono.test.ts(3525,5): error TS2769: No overload matches this call.
  The last overload gave the following error.
    Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string[]'.

These aren't new bugs. The test expects a type error (that's why it has // @ts-expect-error), and both versions find it. But TS 7 reports it on a different line: inside the call, rather than on the line the comment covers. So the comment becomes "unused", which is an error of its own, and the real error is no longer suppressed.

If your tests use @ts-expect-error on multi-line expressions, run tsc after upgrading and move the comments where needed.

Should you upgrade?

  • ✅ Apps and libraries that just run tsc: yes.
  • ✅ Big monorepos, slow CI, a laggy editor: this is where it pays off most.
  • ⚠️ Fix TypeScript 6 deprecation warnings first.
  • ⚠️ Tools that import typescript as a library (some bundler loaders and linters): TS 7.0 doesn't ship the full programmatic API yet; it's planned for 7.1. Check your toolchain before switching.
  • ⚠️ Check your @ts-expect-error lines.

How long does tsc take on your project? Try 7 and share your before/after numbers. 👇

I post one tested coding tip every day on YouTube at Refactorly. The 30-second version of this one is here.

articles.title: My search box scored 1.00 on a query it understood nothing about
articles.description: A visitor typed "18 m high, 8 m wide". The fallback returned a rebar hook table and a brick chart, both at 1.00 confidence. Both matched because their index text contains the string "180".
articles.body_html:
On 21 November someone typed 18米高8米宽 into the search box on my site. That means "18 m high, 8 m wide" — a question about scaffolding, arriving from a comment thread about a job site. The search returned a table of rebar hook lengths and a chart of bricks per cubic metre of masonry.

Both results were served at a relevance score of 1.00.

The query contains no noun. Not one. It is two dimensions and nothing else, and my matcher looked at it and said: perfect match, here you go.

This is about the arithmetic that made that inevitable, why the obvious fixes don't help, and the four-line gate that replaced a scoring problem with a refusal to guess.

The failure has two stages, and the first one behaved correctly

Search on the site is a plain substring AND over an index string per card. Each card carries a data-k attribute — title, category, a one-line description, the slug, and a handful of pinyin and synonym aliases. Stage one requires every whitespace-separated token of the query to appear somewhere in that string.

// stage 1
n = apply(function (key) {
  for (var i = 0; i < toks.length; i++) {
    if (key.indexOf(toks[i]) < 0) return false;
  }
  return true;
});

Chinese has no spaces, so 18米高8米宽 is one token, and no index string contains it. Zero results. That is correct for stage one, and it is why stage two exists: people type questions, the index stores nouns, and substring matching won't bridge that on its own.

Stage two is a 2-gram fallback. Split the query into CJK bigrams and alphanumeric runs, drop segments that appear nowhere in the index, then score every card:

var gs = raw.match(/[a-z0-9]+|[\u4e00-\u9fff]+/g);   // segment the query
// CJK segment → all overlapping 2-grams; ASCII/digits → kept whole
score = hits / valid.length;                          // fraction of grams found
if (max >= 0.5) showEverythingTiedAtMax();

That "drop segments that appear nowhere" step is the clever part, and it is normally what makes this kind of fallback work at all. A user types 一米多重怎么算; 怎么算 exists on no card, so counting it in the denominator would cap every real match at 20%. Filtering noise out of the denominator is what lets the signal win.

On this query, the filter did its job perfectly — and that is the problem. 米高 and 米宽 are not in the index. Neither is anything else. What survived was the digits.

The score is hits / tokens, which rewards queries it understands least

Two grams survived, so the denominator was 2, so one hit scored 0.5 and cleared the threshold. Required matches is always ceil(n/2): four grams need two, two grams need one, and a single-gram query needs a hit to score a flat 1.00.

Read that back: the less of the query the parser could keep, the lower the bar to answer it. Confidence and comprehension move in opposite directions — the exact inversion of what a relevance score should mean.

The index has 238 cards and 4,204 distinct CJK bigrams, and the frequency distribution is brutally top-heavy:

Bigram Cards containing it Share of index
算器 206 86.6%
计算 187 78.6%
用量 64 26.9%
面积 61 25.6%

Every card title ends in "calculator", so any fragment of that word is universal. A two-gram query where one gram is 计算 scores 0.5 everywhere before it has found out what the page is about.

What the two grams actually were

Here is the part I did not expect. The surviving grams were 18 and 8, and two cards contain both. Both contain them because both index strings contain the number 180:

  • the rebar hook page, whose index text includes 180度弯钩 — a 180-degree hook;
  • the brick table, whose index text includes 120 / 180 / 240 — wall thicknesses in millimetres.

18 and 8 are substrings of 180. One page means degrees, the other means millimetres, and the scoring function saw identical evidence in both. The 1.00 was not a measurement of relevance. It was a coincidence of string layout, and it happened to land on exactly the two cards whose numbers differ in unit from the question that was asked.

Digit fragments are rare in the index, which made the coincidence look like a signal:

Fragment Cards containing it Share
18 2 1%
8 5 2%
1 13 5%
5 14 6%

And because the fallback shows everything tied at the maximum in build order rather than by score, the answer was stable, reproducible, and arbitrary. 1.5米 produced seven cards at 1.00 for the same reason: grams 1 and 5, one hit each, seven winners.

Rarity doesn't rescue you

The reflex fix is IDF — weight rare grams up, common grams down. It makes this worse. 18 appears on 2 of 238 cards, so it is maximally rare, so IDF would push its weight to the ceiling and make the wrong answer more confident.

The confusion is between a rare term and a rare substring. 18 is rare because numbers are fragments of larger numbers, not because it carries meaning. A tokenizer that treats digits as units of evidence is measuring typography, not language. Same reason 8 and 800 and 1800 all look like unrelated, highly specific facts.

The gate: does the query still contain a subject?

I stopped trying to make the score smarter and put a check in front of it instead. Strip the units, the dimension words, the numerals and the question particles. If nothing is left, the query is not a document lookup — it is a parameter lookup, and a search box has no business answering it.

var MEASURE = /米|厘米|毫米|公分|吨|公斤|千克|kg|mm|cm|多高|多宽|多长|多重|多厚|多少|几个|几根|几块|几米|[0-9.\s]/g;

function hasSignal(raw) {
  var t = raw.replace(MEASURE, "").replace(/高|宽|长|厚|重|大|小|的/g, "");
  // a CJK noun survived, or an identifier like hrb400 / c30 / pavement
  return /[\u4e00-\u9fff]/.test(t) || /[a-z]{2,}/.test(t);
}

Two details matter. The strip list is deliberately greedy — 高宽长厚重 are the words people use to describe a dimension, and leaving them in would let 18米高 pass as a subject. The second clause keeps real identifiers alive: hrb400 and c30 are not measurements, and killing them would break every steel and concrete query on the site.

When the gate returns false, the fallback does not run, and the UI says nothing was found and offers the category list. Zero results beats a plausible wrong one, because the two failures have different costs. Someone who gets nothing retypes the query. Someone who gets a hook-length table concludes the site doesn't have a scaffolding calculator and leaves.

Measured, before and after

Twenty dimension-only queries — 18米高8米宽, 6米跨度, 4.5米层高, 300高, 0.5米厚, and so on — run against the same 238-card index, with the old fallback and the gated one:

Answered Relevant
Old fallback 19 / 20 0 / 19
Gated 3 / 20 0 / 3

Nineteen out of twenty got an answer, and not one of them was about the right thing. That is the shape of the bug: not a rare wrong answer, but a system that answered almost everything and was almost never right.

I'll be straight about the residual. Three still get through, because 跨度 and 层高 are genuine nouns even though the query is a dimension: 6米跨度 returns four cards, 4.5米层高 returns two (paint coverage and wallpaper, both of which mention ceiling height in passing). And 18米高8米宽间距1.5 returns fourteen, because 间距 survives the strip — it is a real word, and it is also the one word in that sentence that describes a parameter rather than a product. A vocabulary of parameter nouns would fix those. I haven't built it, and I'd rather ship the gate that removes 16 wrong answers than wait for the one that removes 19.

The second-order cost, in the analytics

Every search reports its result count. Zero-result queries are the useful ones: a demand list of things people asked for that the site doesn't have, which I read every morning.

For as long as the fallback answered these queries, they never appeared as misses. The 18 × 8 m scaffold, the 6 m span, the wall thickness — all recorded as successful searches. The bug didn't just serve the wrong page; it deleted the evidence that the page was missing. Two weeks of demand data, silently scored 1.00.

That is the part I'd flag to anyone with a hand-rolled matcher: a false positive in search is also a false negative in your product backlog, and only one of those is visible to the user.

Reproducing it

The harness reads the built index.html, pulls every card's data-k, and runs both versions of the fallback against the same 20 queries:

score = sum(1 for g in valid if g in key) / len(valid)   # identical to the JS
if max_score >= 0.5: winners = [c for c in cards if s(c) >= max_score - 1e-9]

Run it against your own index and look at two numbers: how many cards tie at the maximum, and how many of the query's surviving grams are digits or fragments of digits. If both are non-zero, your fallback is answering questions it cannot read.

The site this came from is jianzhujisuan.com, a set of construction-quantity calculators with 238 tools on the index. The scaffolding page is the one that visitor was actually looking for, and it took a comment-section bug report for the search box to stop hiding it.

The lesson I keep re-learning, in one line: a relevance score is a claim about the query, not about the page. Mine was computed entirely from the page, and so it was 1.00 on a query that had nothing in it to be relevant to.
